title: The Week, Unwrapped: Two Dan Sullivans, a Speed Limit in Orbit and a Factory That Arrived by Rally
dek: The Justice Department sues over a name, Elon Musk blames Ukraine for using its internet in a war, Audi drops by a campaign rally, and France arrests its way through a school protest.
body:
## The Justice Department discovers a second Dan Sullivan

Nine days before the midterms, the federal government has found the real threat to American democracy: a retired teacher named Daniel J. Sullivan [1].

On Thursday, the Justice Department sued Alaska to delay certifying the Senate result if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses to Democrat Mary Peltola, arguing the other Sullivan on the ballot could confuse voters [1]. The suit says "An election result may be impacted by voter confusion" [1]. President Trump said he directed the department to file it [1]. The Alaska Supreme Court ordered the second Sullivan onto the ballot back in June, where he'll appear as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. [1]. In the primary he got about 2.5 percent, while Peltola got about 49.5 and the senator about 41 [1]. So the plan, apparently, is to win a toss-up race by suing the alphabet.

Notre Dame law professor Derek Muller told the AP the suit likely won't survive, because the law it relies on doesn't let the department block certification [1]. Election law scholar Richard Hasen notes the complaint's only legal hook is the preamble of the National Voter Registration Act, and that its request for relief was missing a verb [2]. Losing a verb is rough. Losing 26 straight cases seeking unredacted state voter lists, as the department reportedly has, is a pattern [2].

And that's just Alaska. In California, the department demanded that mail ballots tied to a list of about 20,000 "suspected" noncitizens be set aside; according to Hasen, a county review of 200 names found more than half weren't even registered [2]. The department announced 28 arrests for alleged noncitizen voting, including a pre-dawn raid with armed officers and helicopters [2]. Helicopters. Hasen calls it political theater [2], which is unfair to theater, where at least the props are cheap. Meanwhile, Attorney General Todd Blanche said the department wouldn't get involved in counting or certifying votes absent a "doomsday scenario" [2]. Good news: the doomsday scenario, it turns out, is a guy with the same name.

## Elon Musk finds the speed limit in space

For more than a week, Ukraine's Starlink service was throttled, disrupting its war effort [4]. Ukrainian forces found out the way the rest of us find out about outages: things broke, they called support, and support told them service would be restricted on platforms moving 100 mph or faster [4]. Zelensky disclosed the artificial speed limit on October 17, and the cutoff grounded interceptor drones Ukraine uses against Russian Shahed drones [3].

On Saturday, service was back to full speed [3][4]. Also on Saturday, Elon Musk posted that using Starlink "for offensive drone strikes to kill people" violated its terms of service, and "That loophole was closed last week" [4]. That's an interesting thing to say about an army in the middle of a war, which tends to use its equipment for war.

The week before, Musk had said "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS" [4]. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth denied the U.S. government was responsible [4]. So Musk says it was the government, the government says it wasn't the government, and Musk also says it was Ukraine's own fault. That's three explanations for one speed bump, which is two more than most car companies give you for a recall.

Ukraine's side has notes. A presidential technology adviser, Serhii Beskrestnov, said Starlink in Ukraine has had speed limits since early 2026 and is geofenced off in Russia [3]. "Very strange that Elon Musk does not know about the restrictions on Starlink operations in Ukraine," he said [3]. When the customer knows your terms of service better than the CEO does, maybe it's time to update the FAQ.

## A factory, now with rally

On Saturday at a campaign rally in Perry, Georgia, President Trump announced that Audi will build a plant near Macon, $4.2 billion, 200,000 cars a year [5]. "Think of that," he said [5]. And credit where it's due: Audi confirmed it, with about 4,500 jobs [5]. It's real.

It is also arriving on a schedule. Construction starts in 2027, and production begins in the early 2030s [5]. So the cars come several elections from now, and the announcement came ten days before this one [5]. The Republican candidate for governor called it "the biggest economic deal in Georgia history" [5]. Audi's chairman came on stage to promise "our biggest and most premium SUVs" [5]. A German luxury carmaker doing a cameo at an American midterm rally is the kind of thing that makes you realize corporate press releases now come with walk-up music.

Trump credited his tariffs for the plant [5]. Audi's chairman, for his part, talked SUVs [5]. Somewhere, a Volkswagen accountant is quietly calculating whether building the cars here is cheaper than paying the tariff on the ones built there, which is the most honest economic analysis that will happen at any rally this year.

## Meanwhile, in France

France had another weekend of mass protests over crumbling schools, teacher shortages, the university admissions system and the cost of living [6]. The Interior Ministry counted 410,000 marchers; the CGT union said it was nearly double [6]. Protest math is the one place where the government and the unions agree on exactly one thing: the other side can't count.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said police faced "an extremely elevated level of violence" and that nearly 1,000 people were arrested on Saturday [6]. That follows more than 2,000 taken into custody on October 17 [6]. The movement started in September with high school blockades [6]. Teenagers organizing a national movement over broken buildings and admissions rules, and the headlines so far have mostly been about the police. Somewhere a French civics teacher is grading this, and it's not going well for anybody.

## The bottom line

This week, the government sued over a name, a billionaire blamed a war for using its internet, a carmaker brought its SUVs to a rally, and France arrested its way through a school protest [1][3][5][6]. The only consistent thing in power this week: when something goes wrong, it's always the other Sullivan's fault [1].

de.title: Die Woche, ausgepackt: zwei Dan Sullivans, ein Tempolimit im Orbit und eine Fabrik, die per Wahlkampfauftritt kam
de.dek: Das Justizministerium klagt wegen eines Namens, Elon Musk wirft der Ukraine vor, sein Internet im Krieg zu nutzen, Audi tritt bei einer Wahlkampfveranstaltung auf, und Frankreich verhaftet sich durch einen Schulprotest.
